title: Cross-version tool-call interpreter with probabilistic name resolution
creator: Ava Singh
description: Problem: Customers and OSS clients call Redwood tooling using a mixture of historic 'legacy functions' conventions and newer OpenAI-style 'tools'. Name variants, parameter ordering, and types differ across language SDKs and historical integrations. This causes failures (400/422) or silent misrouted calls when the runtime cannot map the incoming tool descriptor to a hosted tool implementation. Goal: implement a runtime interpreter that tolerates name variants and signature differences, provides deterministic fallback rules, and allows ops to approve or reject probabilistic mappings via an admin flow. The feature should preserve safety and observability while minimizing false positives in production.
background: We already have shims that map a handful of name changes and a compatibility router for some tool-contract variations (existing tickets documented ad-hoc mappings). However, we lack a general, auditable system that: (1) resolves ambiguous tool names (case, punctuation, synonyms), (2) reconciles parameter naming and optionality, and (3) exposes a low-friction migration path for customers moving from legacy functions to the OpenAI-style tool surface.
design_decision: Use a deterministic-first strategy with probabilistic augmentation: build a rules-based resolver (exact, alias, normalized) executed first; when no rule matches, use a lightweight fuzzy matcher that returns candidate mappings with confidence scores. Low-confidence matches are not invoked automatically — they enter a 'suggested mapping' queue for admin approval. High-confidence matches can be auto-applied behind a feature flag with throttled rollout. All mappings are recorded in an audited mapping registry and can be surfaced in the Console for operators.
tradeoffs: 1) Deterministic rules are simple and explainable but require manual upkeep. 2) Fuzzy/probabilistic matching reduces manual work but risks incorrect routing; we mitigate via confidence thresholds, sandboxed canaries, and review UI. 3) Adding this layer increases runtime path complexity and small CPU overhead for name resolution; mitigate with caching and incremental precompilation of mappings. 4) Privacy/security: we must avoid leaking prompt/tool payloads to external ML services; the fuzzy matcher will run locally using token-based similarity or a curated embedding index, not third-party APIs.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 - Resolver core: implement normalization pipeline (strip punctuation, lowercasing, canonical synonyms) + alias table data model in control plane
Phase 1 - Registry: mapping store with versioning, creator, source (auto vs manual), and approval state
Phase 2 - Fuzzy matcher: lightweight token/fuzzy matching library (Levenshtein + token overlap + signal from past telemetry) with confidence score
Phase 2 - Runtime shim: call interception layer that queries resolver and returns unified tool call contract to execution path; no automatic invocation for low-confidence matches
Phase 3 - Admin tooling: Console page for suggested mappings, manual approvals, and bulk alias edits
Phase 3 - Telemetry & metrics: misroute rate, suggestion acceptance rate, false-positive incidents, per-customer mapping counts
Phase 4 - Rollout: feature flag, canary customers, and automated rollback on error thresholds
rollout_plan: Start feature-flagged in runtime-1.22 with resolver disabled by default
Enable fuzzy-suggestion mode for internal accounts and 3 pilot customers
Collect metrics for 2 weeks: suggestion accuracy, manual approvals, invocation failures
If stable, enable auto-apply for high-confidence matches (<0.5% observed misroute rate) behind an opt-in org setting
Full enablement only after Console mapping UI and audit logs are in place
testing_and_metrics: Unit tests for normalization and alias lookup
Integration tests covering: exact match, alias match, fuzzy candidate list, parameter normalization (snake_case vs camelCase), type coercion cases
Chaos tests: simulate missing mapping and ensure safe failure modes (clear error to caller, no silent misinvoke)
E2E scenario tests with sample legacy clients and OpenAI-style tool callers
notes: We should coordinate with SDK teams to publish a recommended alias manifest for popular language SDKs. Plan to add a small admin email notification when a mapping is auto-applied for the first time in a customer org. Keep fuzzy matcher model parameters configurable per-org to allow conservative defaults for high-security customers.
